title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> result: output, not counted
- index variable idx: O(1)
- not counted: input array (modified in place), returned vector
approach: Since every value x lies in [1, n] and n is the array length, each value maps to a unique index x-1. We use the input array itself as a presence marker: when we see value x, we negate nums[x-1]. If nums[x-1] is already negative on a later visit, x is a duplicate. We take abs(nums[i]) before indexing because earlier marks may have flipped the sign of the current cell.
hints: Every value x is in [1, n] where n is the array length. What does that let each value x point to inside the array itself?
Use the array as its own presence marker by negating nums[x-1]. For nums=[4,3,2,7,...], processing 4 flips nums[3] to negative; when 4 is seen again, nums[3] is already negative → duplicate.

**Smallest input** - n=1, no duplicate possible.
`Input: nums = [1]` → `Expected: []`
⚠️ Bug: appending before checking the sign → returns `[1]`

**Adjacent duplicates** - the duplicate sits right next to its first occurrence.
`Input: nums = [1,2,2]` → `Expected: [2]`
⚠️ Bug: using `nums[i]` instead of `abs(nums[i])` for the index → at i=2, nums[2]=-2, idx=-3, out-of-bounds

**All-equal pair** - both slots hold the same value.
`Input: nums = [1,1]` → `Expected: [1]`
⚠️ Bug: marking after the append check instead of before → returns `[]`

**Boundary last element** - duplicate value equals n, pointing at the final cell.
`Input: nums = [2,2]` → `Expected: [2]`
⚠️ Bug: using `abs(nums[i])` as the index (off by one) → accesses nums[2], out-of-bounds

followUps.q: What if each value could appear up to k times instead of at most twice - return values appearing exactly k times?
followUps.a: Replace the sign flip with modular counting: increment nums[x-1] by n each visit, then a value x appears (nums[x-1] / n) times after the pass. Still O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, but you must restore or read counts via division.

followUps.q: What if you must not modify the input array at all?
followUps.a: The negation trick breaks the "no modification" rule, so you fall back to a hash set of seen values, giving O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. There is no known O(1)-space, no-modification solution for the general case.

followUps.q: What if the data arrives as a streaming sequence you can only read once, with n unknown in advance?
followUps.a: You cannot index into a fixed-size array, so keep an unordered_set of seen values; on a repeat, emit the value. Time stays O(n) expected, but auxiliary space becomes O(n) since you may hold up to n/2 distinct seen values.
